old: India experiences a decrease in the demand for steel. CNR is exposed twice: Leer high-vol A coal is gaining traction in Asia, and PAMC high-CV thermal sells into India at ~$60/t (Q2 FY2026 call; the India share of PAMC's ~26–27M t is not disclosed in our sources). A slowdown in Indian steel and construction would hit both met volumes and the thermal export book, the leg that makes up 61% of segment EBITDA in our bear case.

Leer South / longwall events and the Arch–CONSOL merger integration. The met segment rests on two longwalls (Leer and Leer South); Leer South was idled by a fire in 2025 and the $155M insurance settlement flattered results ($125M of it in Q2 FY2026 EBITDA; ex-insurance LTM met EBITDA is ~$129M). Integration is recent: the merger closed in January 2025, the CEO changed in October 2025 (Paul Lang left with ~$8M severance; Jimmy Brock became Chairman and CEO) and board tenure averages under one year. Another longwall event or integration slippage would push met cash cost back above the $86–91/t guidance.

India experiences a decrease in the demand for steel. India and Southeast Asia are where new blast-furnace capacity is being built, and Alpha's export tons priced on Australian indices realized $143.82/t in Q2 FY2026 against $109.08/t for Atlantic-priced tons. If Indian demand slows, the Pacific outlet for US high-vol coal closes, the ~500kt a month of new US high-vol supply (management estimate) competes for Atlantic cargoes, and Alpha's realization falls toward the Atlantic level.

Cost position and liquidity. Alpha is a room-and-pillar and surface miner with the highest cost in the basket: FY2026 Met cost guidance was raised to $103–107/t against a $118.71/t realization in Q2 FY2026. It posted a fifth straight quarterly loss, LTM FCF is about zero (CFO $138M vs capex $140M, FiscalAI), liquidity fell to $447.8M from $476.2M in one quarter, and exports depend on DTA, where a stacker-reclaimer was damaged on 14 June 2026 with no repair date. A further $10/t drop in price costs ~$145M of EBITDA a year, more than the $121M LTM EBITDA.

China continues the acceleration of programs with electric furnaces. Met is the smaller part of CNR (met segment $366M of ~$1.14B segment revenue in Q2 FY2026, 32%) but carries most of the upside in our bull case. More Chinese electric-furnace steel and steel exports cut seaborne coking-coal demand and widen the PLV–high-vol A spread that prices Leer coal. The high-CV thermal leg partly hedges this, since PAMC sells into power and Indian cement rather than steel.

China continues the acceleration of programs with electric furnaces. 50% of Warrior's Q2 FY2026 sales went to Asia, and part of the Q2 price support came from Chinese import demand (the China CFR–Australia FOB arbitrage reopened after being closed for over a year). Global pig iron output fell 1.9% in H1 2026 with China the main source of weakness (World Steel, cited on the Q2 FY2026 call). A structural move of Chinese steel to electric furnaces lowers seaborne coking-coal demand and pushes more cheap Chinese steel into HCC's European and South American customers (35% and 14% of Q2 FY2026 sales).

India experiences a decrease in the demand for steel. India is the growth outlet for Blue Creek: Indian pig iron output rose 2.7% y/y in H1 2026 while global output fell 1.9%, and Blue Creek high-vol A is being sold mostly into the Pacific Basin despite freight to India $13/t (37%) higher y/y. If Indian demand slows, the 5.0M st of Blue Creek tons would have to go to the Atlantic, where the US East Coast HVA index was only 66% of PLV in Q2 FY2026 (92% a year earlier).

Blue Creek ramp and longwall concentration. Warrior mines only with longwalls (Mines 4 and 7 plus Blue Creek), so one adverse-geology event or longwall failure can take 25%+ of production at once. Blue Creek is 5.0M of the 13.0–14.0M st FY2026 guidance (~37%), is still ramping toward its 7.5M st design rate, and its high-vol A mix pulls gross price realization down (66% of PLV in Q2 FY2026 vs 80% a year earlier). A stalled ramp or a longwall outage in 2027 hits claim 3 (2028 cash flow above $1B) directly: at the $40/t bear-case margin, every 1M st lost costs ~$40M of EBITDA.

China continues the acceleration of programs with electric furnaces. Export met revenue was $325M of Alpha's $454M met coal revenue in Q2 FY2026 (72%, FiscalAI), and management blames Chinese steel exports for weak demand at its South American and other customers. More electric-furnace steel in China and more Chinese steel exports keep seaborne met demand weak; with a ~$16/t margin in Q2 FY2026, Alpha has far less room than Warrior to absorb it.

Greater China may be a structural share loss, not a cycle. Revenue fell from $7,545M in FY2024 to $5,847M in FY2026 (-22%) and EBIT from $2,309M to $1,278M (-45%); Q4 FY2026 revenue was down 17% and management expects similar near-term trends. Local brands (Anta, Li Ning) compete on price and cultural relevance. China was 17% of FY2024 geographic segment EBIT ($2,309M of $13,404M); each further $500M of lost China revenue at the FY2026 22% segment margin costs ~$110M of EBIT.

Sportswear and Jordan Streetwear are about half of revenue and management expects both to keep declining through FY2027, improving only in the second half. Sportswear fell double digits in Q4 FY2026. Performance categories are growing (running added ~$1B over five quarters), but they are the smaller half. If lifestyle declines another ~10% a year, performance has to grow ~10% a year just to keep revenue flat at $46.4B, and the base case needs $49.7B by FY2029. UBS has also flagged that wider Jordan distribution and more promotions could weaken the brand's exclusivity.

Tariffs are a recurring cost that the FY2026 numbers hide. The $986M IEEPA refund recognised in Q4 FY2026 added 210bps to FY2026 gross margin (40.8% without it) and $0.52 to EPS ($1.58 without it); over $300M had been collected by 31 May 2026 and the rest (under ~$690M) sat in receivables. Management's FY2027 plan assumes a 15% incremental tariff from August 2026. Each 100bps of gross margin is ~$460M of EBIT, about 16% of FY2026 adjusted EBIT (~$2.8B). Nike's footwear is made mostly in Vietnam, Indonesia and China (hypothesis from prior 10-Ks, not re-checked), so a higher rate or a lost refund claim goes straight to margin.

The Americas brand erosion is structural, not cyclical. The Americas are 69% of LTM revenue and 71% of FY2025 segment operating income, comps have been negative in all six quarters of FY2025 and FY2026 so far and reached -12% in Q2 FY2026, and the core leggings franchise fell ~20%. Competitors (Alo, Vuori, On) take the same premium customer.

Because stores, leases and marketing are fixed, every point of lost revenue falls through at a high rate: Q3 FY2026 operating margin is guided at ~6.5% vs 17% a year earlier. If Americas revenue falls to ~$6.2B, the bear case gives EPS of $7.69 and $76.86 a share, 21% below the price.

China turns from growth engine to drag. China Mainland revenue compounded 45% a year FY2022–FY2025 to $1.75B, with a ~40% segment operating margin, and funded most of the company's growth while the Americas stalled. Comps fell from +26% in Q4 FY2025 to -8% in Q2 FY2026 on brand-sentiment incidents and weaker Tmall events.

Lululemon still plans ~25 international openings in FY2026, many in China. If comps stay negative while the fleet grows, China margins compress and the International growth the base case needs (~5% a year to $4.0B) does not arrive.

Leadership and governance in flux. Three leadership set-ups in one year: Calvin McDonald left in January 2026, interim co-CEOs ran the company for seven months and Heidi O'Neill started on 8 September 2026 with no plan yet published. The board has absorbed a founder proxy fight (Chip Wilson, ~9.1%, two nominees seated in the May 2026 settlement) and an activist holding more than $1B (Elliott) that backed another CEO candidate.

A new CEO under pressure from both may take a large reset (store closures, inventory write-downs, higher marketing) that pushes margins below the base case for longer. Law-firm investigations into the Q2 FY2026 tariff-refund disclosure add litigation noise.

Brand heat in running fades the way it has for other running brands. The Americas are 57.7% of FY2025 sales and wholesale is 58%. In Q2 FY2026, sell-out of On's everyday running franchises in US wholesale was already below plan "in a highly promotional multi-brand marketplace", and Americas growth slowed to 13.0% cc (4.5% reported) from 17.1% cc in Q1. The Base needs sales to grow about 13% a year in CHF to FY2029. If the core franchise loses shelf space, growth drops to high single digits and the multiple de-rates at the same time: the Bear case is $21.85, -26% from $29.55. Lifestyle franchises (CloudTilt +190% in the premium sneaker channel) partly offset this, but fashion demand is less durable than performance demand.

Currency. On reports in CHF, keeps a CHF-heavy overhead base, sells mostly in USD and EUR, and trades in USD. In Q2 FY2026 reported growth was 13.5% against 21.6% at constant currency. In Q2 FY2025, FX drove a CHF -139.9M non-operating result that turned the quarter into a CHF -40.9M net loss. For a USD holder the translation cuts both ways: the Base target is $43.64 at 1.20 USD/CHF (29 September 2026 spot) and $44.96 at the 1.2364 FiscalAI/platform rate, and every 5% move in the franc moves the target by 5%. The margin of safety is only $1.00 below the 0.70 x IVO line, so a small FX move changes its color.

Leadership and control changed in the same year the guide was cut. CEO/CFO Martin Hoffmann left on 1 May 2026, the founders David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti became Co-CEOs while staying Executive Co-Chairmen, and Frank Sluis took his first call as CFO in the quarter FY2026 guidance was cut. Class B voting-rights shares (325.0M) carry about 52% of the votes for about 9.7% of the economics, so outside holders cannot force a change of course. Add tariff exposure: production is concentrated in Vietnam, and the FY2026 guide assumes 20% incremental US tariffs, with refunds not yet quantified. The first $1B buyback is the test of whether the new team allocates capital for per-share value.

Met segment cash cost dropped to $85.65/t in Q2 FY2026 (about −$7/t q/q) after the Leer longwall moved into better seams and Leer South returned; guidance was lowered to $86–91/t. The CEO called the level sustainable. Two more quarters inside the range show the Leer/Leer South problems of 2025 are behind; a jump above $91/t would point to another geology or longwall event.

Cash cost of sales fell to $92.53/t in Q2 FY2026 (−9% y/y) on Blue Creek mix and the 45X credit. Management expects a few dollars per ton of inflation in H2 and has two longwall moves in Q3 and one in Q4. Holding below $100/t confirms that Blue Creek lowered the cost base, which is the cost-advantage pillar of the thesis; a print above $100/t would mean the Q2 figure was mix and credits, not structure.

Met cost of coal sales was $103.07/t in Q2 FY2026 after $107.98 in Q1; FY2026 guidance was raised $7/t at the midpoint to $103–107/t on diesel and supplies. Kingston Wildcat, a new low-vol mine, is ramping in Q3–Q4 FY2026 and should lift the low-vol mix. A Q4 cost at or below $103/t says the new mine offsets inflation; above $107/t says Alpha's cost position keeps deteriorating.

Total liquidity was $447.8M at Q2 FY2026, down from $476.2M at Q1 (cash $307.6M, short-term investments $30.9M, ABL availability $184.3M, less $75M minimum liquidity). LTM FCF is about zero to negative and buybacks continued ($36.7M in H1 FY2026). A drop below $400M while prices stay low would put the no-dilution leg of claim 2 under pressure and should stop buybacks.

CNR returned $68M in Q2 FY2026 ($63M buybacks) and $360M (over 80% of FCF) since February 2025. The $155M Leer South claim is settled, $38M more arrives in Q3, and management said to expect heavier buybacks in Q3–Q4 plus a $75–100M working-capital release. A Q3 return above $100M confirms the framework (~75% of FCF) holds with the cash in hand.

FY2026 guidance was raised to 13.0–14.0M st with Blue Creek at 5.0M st, 90% contracted. Claim 3 of the thesis needs Blue Creek fully commissioned in 2027 and 2028 cash flow above $1B. The FY2027 guidance (with the Q4 FY2026 report, Feb 2027) is the first dated test of the ramp; analysts on the Q2 call referenced 6M st as the target run-rate.

With Blue Creek capex complete, Q2 FY2026 FCF was $103.4M and cash reached $302M. The CFO said the target is $350–400M of cash (~$500M total liquidity) and that buybacks are one of the levers once there. HCC has only paid a $0.08 quarterly dividend since FY2023. A buyback authorization or special dividend tests whether management returns the Blue Creek cash rather than holding it.

Claim 2 of the thesis rests on the domestic band (~30% of production) priced the prior Q3/Q4, which is immune to the weak export index. For 2026 domestic committed tons slipped to 3.8M t from 4.1M t because customers did not declare options. Negotiations for 2027 are under way; management said US blast furnaces are running and low-vol demand should be good. The Q3 or Q4 FY2026 report will show the 2027 committed and priced position.

Management expects 8.5–9.0M t from the Leer complex; 8.7M coking tons are contracted for 2026. FY2027 guidance (Feb 2027) is the first full-year plan without the 2025 Leer South fire and with the merger a year old. Meeting both volume and cost shows the Arch assets integrated into CONSOL's operating practices; a lower volume or higher cost would weaken the met leg that carries most of the upside.

Nike is employing same playbook Adidas used to stabilize its China business: local autonomy, design "in and for" China, and a territorial expansion drive. The precedent suggests a 2y lag between the trough and the 1st Q of positive growth, with full recovery taking over 3Y and no guarantee of returning to previous peaks. Metrics: (1) Q currency-neutral growth in Greater China, (2) signs of local traction, reported by Hill in "must-win doors" (high-single-digit sales growth in investment locations); and (3) stabilization of China EBIT (which fell from $1.60B to $1.28B between FY25 and FY26).

Management guided Q1 FY2027 (reported 1 October 2026) to revenue down low to mid single digits and gross margin "slightly positive" year over year, with an incremental tariff rate of 15% from August. Q1 FY2026 printed $11,720M of revenue at a 42.2% gross margin ($4,943M). This is the first quarter without the IEEPA refund distortion and the first test of claim 2: margin recovering while tariffs stay in the cost base. A miss here would say the discount clean-up is not yet offsetting tariffs.

Americas comps went -1%, -3%, -5%, -2% through FY2025, then -6% in Q1 FY2026 and -12% in Q2 FY2026. Management guided Q3 North America revenue down mid-teens and said August started slowly, so the guide already assumes a worse quarter.

A Q3 print at -12% or better, with revenue at or above the $2.29–2.32B guide, would be the first sign that the trough is Q2–Q3 FY2026 and that the base case's Americas floor near $7.0B is reachable. A worse print moves the case toward the bear.

China comps went from +26% in Q4 FY2025 to +13% in Q1 FY2026 and -8% in Q2 FY2026, which management attributed to negative social-media commentary, the Great Wall event and a weaker Tmall 6.18. Guidance still has China revenue up high single digits for FY2026 on store growth.

China was 19% of FY2025 segment operating income at a 40% segment margin. Positive comps by Q4 FY2026 (which includes the 11.11 event) would show the damage was sentiment, not a lost market position.

In Q2 FY2026 management cut FY2026 constant-currency growth guidance from "at least 23%" (reiterated on 12 May 2026) to "low 20s", raised gross margin to at least 65% and kept adjusted EBITDA at 19.5–20%. It said Q3 growth will be lower than Q4 because the rest of the wholesale sell-in cuts land in Q3. H1 FY2026 grew 21.6% cc in Q2 and 26.4% in Q1. Hitting the reset guide in the first year under the new Co-CEOs and CFO tells us whether the Q2 cut was a one-off correction or the first of several. Tariff refunds, which management expects to book from Q3, are excluded from the guide and should be stripped out when checking it.

Wholesale grew 25.1% cc in Q1 FY2026 and 12.7% cc in Q2 as On held back sell-in to US partners where sell-out of everyday running franchises lagged. Cloudsurfer 3 (first shoe on the Surreal superfoam) goes to run-specialty stores in October 2026 with a three-month exclusive, rolls out broadly in January 2027, then Cloudsurfer Max 2 in April and a Cloudflow relaunch. Management says every everyday running franchise moves to the new foams within about 14 months. If wholesale re-accelerates, claim 1 holds and the moat is intact; if it does not, the bear case starts to apply.

The FY2026 gross-margin guide was raised to at least 65% only because of DTC mix, per the CFO. Inventory was CHF 472.9M at Q2 FY2026, up 31% year over year against 13.5% reported sales growth; management put this down to volume and FX. If the US wholesale reset needs clearance or markdowns, or DTC growth slows from 34.3% cc, gross margin falls back toward the FY2025 level of 62.8%. That is the first number the bear case needs.

Nike holds an Investor Day on 16–17 November 2026, the first under Hill, with a new CFO (David Denton appears as EVP CFO in September 2026 filings, after Matt Friend's departure was announced on the Q4 FY2026 call). Management has so far only spoken of "a trajectory to get back to double-digit margins". A target with a date, a gross margin bridge and a capital return policy would make claims 2 and 3 checkable; a vague deck or a dividend reset would weaken them.

In FY2026 dividends paid were $2,407M against free cash flow of $2,184M (OCF $2,868M less capex $684M), with $986M of non-cash tariff refund in earnings and part of it still in receivables. Bank of America cut its EPS estimate to $1.43 on 29 Sep 2026 (press reports label it fiscal 2026, which has already been reported at $2.10, so it is most likely FY2027 — unverified), implying a payout above 100%. A second year of dividends above FCF would mean the payout is funded from the $9.0B of cash and short-term investments and would put the dividend and the buyback restart in question.

Heidi O'Neill started on 8 September 2026 and will present FY2027 guidance with Q4 FY2026 results (March 2027; management said square footage for FY2027 will be given then). This is the first read on whether she resets the cost base (stores, pop-ups, marketing) or chases revenue with spending.

The base case needs operating margin to bottom near 13% and recover to 15.5% by FY2029. A FY2027 guide at or above 13% ex one-offs, with a stated plan to cut fixed cost, supports it; a guide below 12% or a large restructuring charge without a margin path breaks claim 2.

Management guided FY2026 buybacks in line with FY2025 (~$1.2B) and had $713M left on the authorization at Q2 FY2026. H1 FY2026 buybacks were $707M against FCF of $312M, and FY2026 FCF will be squeezed by a Q3 operating margin guided at ~6.5%.

If the full-year buyback reaches ~$1.2B while FCF stays under $900M, cash falls toward $1.0B and the buyback becomes a balance-sheet decision rather than an allocation of surplus cash, which breaks claim 3 and turns the cashflow pillar red.

In September 2026 the board authorized On's first buyback: up to $1B of Class A shares through December 2029, about 10% of the $9.9B market cap at $29.55. Until now the class-A-equivalent count has only risen, from 316.5M in FY2022 to 334.2M in Q2 FY2026 (+1.5% a year), from stock compensation (CHF 72M LTM). With CHF 1,284M of cash and short-term investments and LTM FCF of CHF 438M, a quarter of the program by end FY2027 is affordable without borrowing. Buying well below the Base IVO of $43.64 is accretive. Not buying would say management does not see the value, or wants the cash for stores.

Met coal is a rare and limited material, is input for making steel and ore and exportable production exists only in a few geographies (Australia, Apalaches, Western Canada, etc). Also there exists a supply asymmetry. The dynamic is when a mine closes, the team retires and sells its assets, so there are high entry barriers. The current macro situation sets a low met coal price since 2024, the next boom could "may last for a while", and current companies could experience high earnings.

According to Pabrai citing Ipsco (2005), "low risk coupled with high uncertainty can lead to high rewards": cyclical, uncertain in future earnings, but with cash and contracted flows that covered almost the entire share price. Met coal companies replicates this DNA.

In met coal, the domestic band approximately 30% of production sold at prices fixed in Q3 of the previous year is profitable and immune to the weak index (Q2-2025). The balance sheet acts as a survival cushion. AMR operates with a minimum cash target; net cash reached a peak and ceased buybacks as soon as it saw weakness in Q1-2024. This buys it time to weather the downturn without dilution or bankruptcy.

Furthermore, some of the companies in the baskets have aggressive buybacks at unpopular prices. It's the cornerstone of value creation: in four years, Alpha's diluted share count fell by 32%, with a declared commitment to returning all capital through share buybacks.

AMR and HCC as complementary bets.

Warrior (HCC) = the lowest cost/highest leverage to profit. Longwall miner, bottom quartile of the global cost curve, Blue Creek delivered on budget and ahead of schedule, near the Port of Mobile with a dual rail/barge option. If its mines run normally, it is "virtually guaranteed to be profitable." Its Achilles' heel: it is purely longwall, so a setback could hit 25%+ of production at once. Quantified catalyst: Blue Creek fully commissioned in 2027, with 2028 cash flows that could exceed $1 billion against a market cap of $2.7 billion.

Alpha (AMR), the highest survival/longevity/optionality. Room and pillar (more expensive), farther from the port, dependent on a single rail line. But its disadvantage of having small mines is also an advantage: it can turn production on and off according to demand, has its own blending terminal, buys coal from small producers in Central Appalachia to refine blends, and can hire distressed miners during lean times. The thesis statement: "Alpha could be producing met coal 75-100 years from now – decades after Warrior ceases to exist."

A premium, vertically integrated athletic apparel brand bought at a trough. About 90% of FY2025 revenue went through its own stores (45%) and e-commerce (44%), there is no financial debt, and LTM ROIC is still 26% (FiscalAI). The damage is concentrated in the Americas, 69% of LTM revenue and 71% of FY2025 segment operating income, where comparable sales fell 12% in Q2 FY2026, leggings fell ~20% and newness is not selling. China Mainland, the growth engine (revenue CAGR +45% FY2022–FY2025), turned to -8% comps. The bet is that this is a product and execution failure that a new CEO (Heidi O'Neill, in the seat since 8 September 2026) and a board reshaped after the Chip Wilson settlement can fix, not a permanent loss of the brand to Alo, Vuori or On.

Valued on FY2029 EPS at 12x, not on a return to peak margins. Base case: revenue $10.8B (Americas $6.8B, International $4.0B), roughly flat against the FY2026 guide of $10.35–10.50B; operating margin 15.5%, against ~13.3% implied by FY2026 guidance ex the IEEPA refund and a 3Y average of 21.9%; 30% tax and 95M diluted shares give EPS of $12.56 and $150.67 per share. At $96.87 the stock trades at 7.9x LTM EPS of $12.21 (which includes a $0.86 one-off tariff refund) and ~10x the FY2026 guide midpoint of $9.61. The return does not need margins to recover to the old 20%+: it needs earnings to stop falling and the multiple to move from a distressed ~8–10x to 12x, which is still below any year-end P/E since FY2021 (13.2x at FY2025, 28.3x at FY2024).

Cash generation and a net-cash balance sheet pay for the wait. FCF was positive in every year FY2021–FY2025 (range $328M–$1,644M) and is $1,354M LTM; cash is $1.39B with zero borrowings and ~$600M of undrawn revolver. Buybacks cut shares outstanding from 123.3M at FY2021 to 106.6M at Q2 FY2026 (-14%), with $713M left on the authorization and FY2026 repurchases guided in line with FY2025 ($1.2B). The base case only assumes ~3%/yr of net share reduction to 95M by FY2029, funded from FCF. The weak spot is discipline: buybacks exceeded FCF in FY2024 ($1.67B vs $1.58B), FY2025 ($1.21B vs $0.92B) and H1 FY2026 ($707M vs $312M), and $1.67B was spent in FY2024 at prices 2–4x today's.
Americas comparable sales stay at -8% or worse for four more consecutive quarters (through Q2 FY2027), or FY2027 Americas revenue comes in below $6.5B (vs $7.85B in FY2025).
FCF below $700M in FY2027, or cash below $1.0B together with new borrowings to keep the buyback going, or diluted shares still above 100M at FY2028 year end.

NKE is the largest athletic footwear and apparel brand, with $46.4B of FY2026 revenue ($29.5B footwear, $13.4B apparel, $2.2B equipment) and about 60% of it sold through wholesale. It is bought at a margin trough that is largely self-inflicted: the FY2020–FY2024 push to NIKE Direct cut wholesale doors, leaned on a few lifestyle franchises (Air Force 1, Dunk, Jordan 1) and left the performance pipeline thin; Greater China and tariffs came on top. EBIT margin fell from 14.3% in FY2022 to 6.1% in FY2026 excluding the $986M IEEPA tariff refund. Under Elliott Hill's "Win Now" plan wholesale grew 4% in FY2026, North America wholesale grew 10% in Q4 FY2026, running posted five straight quarters of double-digit growth and classic franchises were cut by more than $2B. The thesis buys the brand's normalized earnings power, not the FY2026 trough.

Valuation anchors on FY2029 EPS rebuilt from margins, not on a return to the FY2021 peak. Base case: revenue $49.7B (2.3% a year from FY2026, after the decline guided for the first half of FY2027), gross margin 42.5% against 40.8% adjusted in FY2026 and 44.6% in FY2024, SG&A at 33% of revenue against 34.7%, so an EBIT margin of 9.5%. That is $3.77B of net income, $2.54 of EPS on 1,480M shares and $50.90 per share at 20x, below the ~30x NKE averaged over the last 12 quarters. The return comes from the E: at $35.84 the stock trades at 17x reported and ~23x adjusted FY2026 EPS ($1.58), so the multiple does little of the work. TSOH's case ($97 at 28x FY2031 EPS) is the upside reference, not the base.

The balance sheet buys time for the turnaround. At the end of FY2026 NKE held $9.0B of cash and short-term investments against $7.9B of notes, $1.1B of net cash before $3.1B of lease liabilities, with no convertibles. Buybacks fell from $4.0–5.5B a year in FY2022–FY2024 to $146M in FY2026, while the $1.64 annual dividend (4.6% yield at $35.84) cost $2.41B, more than the $2.18B of free cash flow. The return is the dividend plus the EPS recovery: at a 9.5% EBIT margin our estimate is free cash flow near $4B a year, covering the dividend about 1.6x and allowing buybacks to restart. Stock-based compensation of ~$715M a year means buybacks first have to absorb dilution before the share count falls.

Revenue is still down year over year on a currency-neutral basis in Q3 and Q4 FY2027 (the half management says should improve), or Greater China keeps falling more than 10% a year through FY2027, or performance categories (running, training, football) stop growing.
Gross margin excluding one-off tariff items is below 41% for FY2027 as a whole, or EBIT margin excluding one-offs is below 7% in FY2027, meaning the tariff and promotion cost is not being recovered.
Free cash flow stays below dividends paid (~$2.4B) in both FY2027 and FY2028, net cash excluding leases turns into net debt above $2B, or the dividend is cut.

On is a premium performance-running brand that grew net sales from CHF 725M in FY2021 to CHF 3,014M in FY2025 (3Y CAGR +35.1% from FY2022) while gross margin rose from 59.4% to 62.8%, and to 64.8% LTM at Q2 FY2026. It grew at full price, not through discounting. The mix moved toward the channels and regions that earn more: DTC went from 36.4% of sales in FY2022 to 41.8% in FY2025 and 45.7% in Q2 FY2026, and APAC from 6.6% to 17.0% (over 20% in Q1 and Q2 FY2026). The stock fell from $50.63 (8 January 2026) to $26.76 (15 September 2026) after Q2 FY2026, when management cut FY2026 constant-currency growth guidance from "at least 23%" to "low 20s" because US wholesale sell-out of everyday running shoes came in below plan and On held back sell-in. The thesis buys a brand whose own channel says demand is intact (DTC +34.3% cc in Q2 FY2026), at a price that treats the wholesale pause as the start of a structural slowdown.

Valuation is anchored to FY2029 earnings at 20x P/E, about the current LTM multiple (20.8x on IFRS net income of CHF 396M) and far below the FY2023–FY2025 average (~73x on FiscalAI year-end figures). The return has to come from the E, not from a re-rating. The base case haircuts the 2029 targets set at the 22 September 2026 Investor Day (net sales of at least CHF 5.6B, gross margin of at least 65%, adjusted EBITDA margin of at least 22%): CHF 5.0B of sales, 64% gross margin, 49% SG&A, 15% EBIT margin, 20% normalized tax and 330M shares give CHF 1.82 of EPS, CHF 36.4 per share and $43.6 at 1.20 USD/CHF. Net cash of CHF 1,284M (cash plus short-term investments, no financial debt) is not added. On reports in CHF and trades in USD: in Q2 FY2026 the franc cut reported growth to 13.5% from 21.6% at constant currency, and the translation into dollars is part of the bet.

The return comes from compounding EPS through mix and operating leverage, funded by the business itself. DTC is planned to reach 50% of sales by 2029, with owned stores going from 80 to 180. Apparel (+56.2% cc in Q2 FY2026) and APAC (+54.7% cc) grow faster than the core. SG&A at 51.0% of sales LTM should give back two points as distribution efficiencies continue (10.0% of sales in Q2 FY2026). The business is asset-light: capex is 2.7% of sales, LTM free cash flow is CHF 438M and ROIC is 36% (FiscalAI). In September 2026 On authorized its first buyback, up to $1B through December 2029, about 10% of the $9.9B market cap at $29.55. That is enough to stop the ~1.5% a year share creep from stock compensation (FY2022–FY2025) and is accretive at today's price.

DTC constant-currency growth below 15% for two consecutive quarters, or wholesale constant-currency growth still below 10% in Q2 FY2027 after the broad Cloudsurfer 3 rollout in January 2027, or quarterly gross margin below 63% as markdowns show up.

FY2027 reported net sales below CHF 3.9B (a growth path under 12% a year), or FY2027 EBIT margin below 13% because SG&A stays at 52% of sales or more while stores and marketing absorb the gross-margin gains.
Class-A-equivalent share count above 334.2M at the end of FY2027, or cash plus short-term investments below CHF 1.0B at the end of FY2027 with less than 25% of the buyback executed.
